paper_title: SkinMind: Equipping Agentic RAG with Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Reliable Dermatology AI

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reliable dermatology AI requires access to verifiable evidence distributed across heterogeneous textual and visual sources. However, conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically relies on one-shot retrieval from flat corpora, limiting its ability to adapt retrieval granularity, explore multi-hop relations, and integrate multimodal clinical evidence. We introduce SkinMind, a multimodal agentic RAG framework that equips policy models with human-inspired graph probing for autonomous evidence seeking. SkinMind organizes retrieval as an iterative interaction between an orchestrator and a graph environment. Through eight hierarchical graph-probing tools, the orchestrator progressively identifies relevant entities, inspects node-level information, traverses relations and paths, and retrieves source-text and visual evidence. This progressive-disclosure design allows the model to adaptively determine the retrieval modality, exploration direction, and evidence granularity while constructing a query-specific evidence subgraph. To support autonomous graph probing, we construct SkinMind-KG from a 62M-token corpus of dermatology guidelines and textbooks and 423K images, guided by a dermatologist-informed schema and a conflict-resolution mechanism. The resulting graph contains over 1.0M nodes and 2.0M edges, unifying textual, relational, and visual evidence for retrieval. Across six dermatology VQA benchmarks and two policy-model settings, SkinMind improves the average score over direct answering by 8.70 and 8.89 points with GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash, respectively, while consistently outperforming competing RAG methods. Together, SkinMind and SkinMind-KG provide an effective foundation for evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning in dermatology.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in language understanding, visual perception, and multi-step reasoning, showing considerable potential for addressing complex real-world tasks [28, 6, 12, 27, 33, 37, 1]. Dermatology represents particularly promising application: many skin conditions are visually observable, and patients increasingly seek convenient access to professional medical guidance through online consultations. Accordingly, medical and dermatology-specific MLLMs have shown potential across tasks such as visual question answering, diagnostic decision-making, and treatment recommendation [10, 17, 16, 5, 31, 29, 44, 22]. Despite this promise, their deployment in safety-critical healthcare settings remains challenging. First, they may 1 SkinMind: Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Dermatology AI generate fluent but factually incorrect statements, potentially leading to harmful clinical decisions. Second, their parametric knowledge is acquired from static training corpora and cannot be readily updated as clinical evidence and guidelines evolve. Third, their responses often lack verifiable references to supporting medical evidence, substantially limiting their reliability and interpretability. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) offers promising means of mitigating these limitations by grounding model responses in external, authoritative, and traceable medical evidence [9, 8, 13, 30, 35, 23, 36, 25, 24, 20, 3, 15]. Conventional RAG systems, however, typically perform one-shot retrieval over flat collection of textual chunks, presenting two limitations for complex medical reasoning [14]. First, one-shot retrieval relies solely on the initial query and cannot adapt to information needs that emerge during multi-step reasoning. Second, flat-chunk retrieval often provides fragmented evidence with insufficient relational context while introducing irrelevant information. Addressing the first limitation requires adaptive, multi-round retrieval, whereas addressing the second calls for structured representation of external medical knowledge. Figure 1: Performance comparison across six dermatology VQA benchmarks using Gemini-2.5-Flash as the policy model. SkinMind consistently outperforms direct answering and LightRAG. Recent agentic RAG methods seek to address the first limitation by interleaving reasoning with iterative retrieval [8, 4]. Rather than relying on fixed set of documents retrieved upfront, the model dynamically determines when additional evidence is needed and formulates new queries based on its intermediate reasoning state. Nevertheless, because these methods typically operate over isolated text chunks, they do not fully resolve the fragmentation and loss of relational context inherent in flat-text retrieval. Graph-based RAG improves upon flat-text retrieval by organizing knowledge into entities and relations [9, 13, 43]. However, many existing methods still treat the graph primarily as retrieval index, selecting entities or subgraphs through embedding similarity or predefined expansion rules. Although the knowledge is graph-structured, the graph itself is rarely exposed to the model for interactive exploration. This contrasts with human-inspired evidence-seeking process, in which reasoner begins with relevant concept, inspects its relations, follows informative paths, and adapts the exploration as new information emerges. This process follows the principle of progressive disclosure [32], whereby lightweight structural cues guide navigation, while detailed descriptions or source content are accessed only when needed. Compared with retrieving fixed candidate set, such navigation allows the retrieval path, scope, and granularity to evolve with the reasoning process, facilitating the flexible construction of query-specific evidence subgraphs while reducing irrelevant context. Inspired by this human-like evidence-seeking process, we propose SkinMind, multimodal agentic RAG framework for autonomous and reliable dermatology assistance. Rather than treating the knowledge graph as static retrieval index, SkinMind exposes it as an interactive environment and equips the agent with eight specialized graph-probing tools for interleaved reasoning and retrieval of textual, relational, and visual evidence. Given clinical query, the agent autonomously identifies relevant entry nodes, inspects their relations, follows informative paths, and progressively accesses node descriptions, source content, and clinical images as needed. To provide comprehensive and traceable foundation of domain-specific evidence, we construct SkinMind-KG, large-scale heterogeneous dermatology knowledge graph containing over 1 million nodes and 2 million edges across 23 core entity types and 25 core relation types. Notably, SkinMind-KG explicitly links 301,561 2 SkinMind: Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Dermatology AI images to disease entities, providing rich visualconceptual associations for multimodal evidence seeking. We conduct extensive experiments on six public dermatology VQA benchmarks spanning morphology recognition, disease diagnosis, and clinical reasoning in both closedand open-ended settings. As illustrated in Fig. 1, SkinMind consistently outperforms direct answering across all six benchmarks, with gains of 4.119.7 points under Gemini-2.5-Flash. More broadly, across both policy-model settings, it surpasses LightRAG by an average of 5.75 points with GPT-5.4-mini and 3.60 points with Gemini-2.5Flash. These results suggest that adaptive graph exploration can support more effective use of external knowledge and improve multimodal clinical reasoning. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We propose SkinMind, multimodal agentic RAG framework that treats knowledge graph as an interactive environment, enabling interleaved reasoning and adaptive evidence seeking through eight graph-probing tools. We construct SkinMind-KG, large-scale heterogeneous dermatology knowledge graph comprising over 1 million nodes and 2 million edges, with more than 300,000 images explicitly linked to disease entities. Extensive experiments on six dermatology VQA benchmarks across two policy-model settings demonstrate that SkinMind consistently outperforms direct answering and competing RAG methods, validating the effectiveness of adaptive graph exploration for evidence-grounded multimodal clinical reasoning.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Retrieval-Augmented Generation. RAG augments language models with evidence from external corpora [21]. Adaptive methods interleave reasoning and retrieval, respond to generation uncertainty, incorporate self-critique, or route queries among retrieval strategies [34, 19, 3, 18]. GraphRAG, LightRAG, and HippoRAG organize evidence through entity graphs, community summaries, and associative retrieval [9, 13, 20]. Think-on-Graph 2.0 alternates graph and document retrieval, while Medical Graph RAG integrates medical sources and controlled vocabularies [24, 36]. Agentic approaches give models control over evidence acquisition: A-RAG exposes hierarchical passage-search interfaces, whereas RAGentA coordinates retrieval, answer generation, and verification across agents [8, 4]. SkinMind combines these directions by exposing heterogeneous multimodal graph as an interactive environment. Its policy model selectively accesses nodes, relations, paths, source passages, and images at the granularity needed for each question. Multimodal Models in Dermatology. SkinGPT-4 adapts visual language model for interactive dermatology, while PanDerm provides domain-specific visual pretraining [44, 40]. Derm1M and MM-Skin supply large imagetext resources for cross-modal representation, retrieval, and dermatology-specific visionlanguage modeling [39, 41]. DermoGPT emphasizes morphology-grounded diagnostic reasoning [29]. Tool-augmented systems complement these models with external memory and specialized components. SkinGPT-X coordinates specialist agents with an evolving case memory, while DermAgent combines perception tools, case and guideline retrieval, disease taxonomy, and evidence auditing [5, 22]. SkinMind uses source-linked dermatology graph as its central retrieval environment, allowing the policy model to select the modality, relation, and evidence granularity during inference. This external knowledge can be updated independently of the policy model and traced to its supporting sources. 3 SkinMind: Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Dermatology AI Figure 2: Overview of SkinMind. The orchestrator adaptively explores SkinMind-KG through hierarchical graph-probing tools to construct query-specific evidence subgraphs for response generation.

sections.title: 3.1 Overview
sections.content: SkinMind is multimodal agentic RAG framework equipped with specialized suite of graph-probing tools for interleaved reasoning and evidence retrieval over dermatology-specific graph environment. Given clinical query, optionally accompanied by an image, SkinMind first routes the query through slowfast reasoning mechanism. Queries that can be answered reliably using the orchestrators internal knowledge are handled by the fast path, whereas queries requiring external evidence, multimodal retrieval, or multi-step reasoning are directed to the slow path. The slow path implements an iterative Agentic RAG loop with four components: an orchestrator, suite of graph-probing tools, graph-based environment, and context manager. The orchestrator acts as the central policy model: it reasons over the current context, selects and invokes appropriate tools, and incorporates the returned observations into subsequent decisions. Once sufficient evidence has been collected, it terminates the interaction loop and generates an evidence-grounded response for the user.

sections.title: 3.4 Hierarchical Graph-Probing Interfaces
sections.content: SkinMind equips the orchestrator with eight graph-probing tools for retrieving and exploring textual, relational, and visual evidence in SkinMind-KG. As summarized in Table 1, six tools support textual retrieval and graph exploration, while two tools support visual retrieval and inspection. Following the principle of progressive disclosure [32, 8], the interfaces initially return compact retrieval results and expose more detailed attributes, relations, and source evidence only when requested, thereby reducing unnecessary context overhead. sections.title: 4.1 Knowledge Graph Construction
sections.content: We construct the textual component of SkinMind-KG from large-scale dermatology corpus comprising 227 clinical guidelines and 542 textbooks published since 2015. We collected dermatology guidelines and textbooks from international online sources, selecting the latest available guideline versions and textbook editions at the time of collection. We parse the raw documents using MinerU [26] 6 SkinMind: Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Dermatology AI Figure 3: Construction and semantic organization of SkinMind-KG. The ontology-guided pipeline integrates knowledge with conflict resolution, while UMAP projections of entity and relation embeddings reveal clusters across semantic categories. and employ lightweight LLM to extract document-level metadata, including titles, authors, publishers, publication years, and editions. To establish an authoritative disease taxonomy, we adopt the PanDerm ontology [40], which comprises 127 disease concepts and their curated hierarchical relationships. We encode these relationships as IS_SUBTYPE_OF relations and preload the resulting hierarchy into SkinMind-KG as its initial taxonomic backbone. Through iterative consultations with senior dermatologists, we further define schema containing 23 entity types and 25 relation types to guide information extraction. Following LightRAG [13], we segment the approximately 62M token corpus into chunks with length of 1,200 tokens. GPT-5.4-mini is then used to extract entities, relations, and their descriptions from each chunk according to the predefined schema. During corpus extraction, the initial disease hierarchy can be extended with additional disease entities and subtype relations. Entity and relation extraction is restricted to statements explicitly supported by the source text. The source context guides the interpretation of clinical qualifiers and the polarity of these statements. Extracted entities and textual relations retain links to their supporting source chunks, which preserve document-level provenance. Through these links, the orchestrator can retrieve supporting passages and their document identifiers using read_chunks when node-level descriptions are insufficient, providing access to the original clinical context. Conflict Detection and Resolution. Integrating heterogeneous sources may introduce contradictory claims about the same entity or relation. We therefore incorporate detect-then-resolve procedure into the construction pipeline. conflict is identified only when two claims make contradictory assertions about the same fact under the same clinical context. Claims associated with different clinical contexts are retained as context-specific evidence rather than treated as conflicts. For each detected conflict, Gemini-3.1-Pro [12] formulates targeted queries and retrieves relevant evidence through Google Search. It then evaluates the retrieved evidence to determine whether the conflict can be reliably resolved. Resolvable cases are automatically reconciled, whereas ambiguous cases are referred to domain experts. In total, the procedure processed 1,375 description-level conflicts, automatically resolving 1,366 cases (99.3%) and referring the remaining nine for expert review. The overall procedure is illustrated in Figure 3(a). Visual Modality Integration. After constructing the textual graph, we augment SkinMind-KG with 423,016 image nodes from Derm1M [39], most of which are accompanied by disease labels. To integrate these images into the graph, we align their disease labels with textual graph nodes of type Disease through three-stage procedure. First, normalized image labels are matched exactly against the names of disease nodes. Second, for unmatched labels, Qwen3-Embedding-4B [42] is used to retrieve the top-10 semantically closest disease nodes. Third, GPT-5.4-mini disambiguates among these candidates and determines whether reliable label-to-node alignment can be established. Based on the resulting 7 SkinMind: Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Dermatology AI alignments, image nodes are connected to the corresponding disease nodes through ILLUSTRATED_BY relations. Images without reliable alignment remain unlinked to disease nodes. To support multimodal retrieval, the images and their associated textual labels are encoded using the visual and textual branches of DermLIP [39], respectively. The resulting representations are indexed to support text-to-image and image-to-image retrieval over the image nodes.

sections.title: 4.2 Graph Statistics and Structural Characteristics
sections.content: The resulting knowledge graph, SkinMindKG, is multimodal, heterogeneous graph containing 1,006,079 nodes and 2,038,419 edges. The 23 core entity types account for 99% of all non-image nodes, while the 25 core relation types account for 99% of all edges excluding ILLUSTRATED_BY. The graph includes 423,016 image nodes, of which 301,561 are connected to disease nodes through ILLUSTRATED_BY relations, providing explicit associations between clinical images and dermatological concepts. SkinMind-KG is unweighted and undirected. Its largest connected component contains 80.0% of all nodes and 99.5% of all edges, indicating that nearly all relational evidence is organized within shared connected subgraph. Table 2 reports the node and edge counts, degree distribution, and connected-component statistics. The average degree is 4.05; among non-isolated nodes, the median and 99th-percentile degrees are 1 and 47, respectively, while the maximum degree is 64,345. This variation in neighborhood size motivates relation-level probing to guide selective neighbor expansion, enabling the orchestrator to adapt the breadth of exploration to the local graph structure.

sections.title: 5.2 Main Results
sections.content: Table 3 presents the main experimental results across six benchmarks. We highlight three key observations. SkinMind delivers consistent performance gains. SkinMind consistently outperforms the corresponding Direct Answer baseline. With GPT-5.4-mini, it improves the average score from 59.20 to 67.90, gain of 8.70 points; with Gemini-2.5-Flash, it increases the score from 60.53 to 69.42, gain of 8.89 points. Most retrieval-augmented methods also improve over direct answering, supporting the value of SkinMind-KG as an external knowledge source. Notably, SkinMind outperforms the competing RAG methods under both policy-model settings, indicating that adaptive graph probing enables more effective use of this knowledge. Adaptive graph probing enables more effective retrieval. Compared with LightRAG, SkinMind improves the average score by 5.75 points with GPT-5.4-mini and 3.60 points with Gemini-2.5-Flash. Meanwhile, the gains of other RAG methods vary across benchmarks and policy models, suggesting that retrieval effectiveness depends not only on access to external knowledge but also on how that knowledge is explored. SkinMind adaptively selects entry nodes, probes relations, and traverses paths to gather query-specific textual and visual evidence at the required granularity. SkinMind is competitive with strong standalone reference models. Although not directly comparable, standalone models provide useful reference points. SkinMind with GPT-5.4-mini achieves an average score of 67.90, comparable to GPT-5.5s 68.08, while outperforming DermoGPT-RL, SkinVLPubMM, and Lingshu-32B by 1.36, 16.35, and 26.00 points, respectively. This result highlights the effectiveness of graph-based evidence seeking in narrowing the gap between the policy model and stronger standalone models.

Together, these capabilities allow the orchestrator to adapt both the evidence source and the retrieval depth to the diagnostic query. 5.

sections.title: Illustrative Case Study
sections.content: Figure 4: An illustrative graph-probing trajectory of SkinMind. By iteratively retrieving visual and textual evidence and comparing plausible diagnoses, SkinMind correctly identifies lichen amyloidosis, whereas Gemini-2.5-Flash and LightRAG produce incorrect predictions. Figure 4 illustrates reasoning trajectory of SkinMind for dermatological diagnosis. Given clinical image and multiple-choice question, SkinMind progressively retrieves visually similar cases, extracts dermatological concepts, and explores relevant disease nodes to gather supporting evidence and eliminate competing diagnoses. By integrating the observed reddish-brown hyperpigmented papules and macules, coalescing lesions, and signs of chronic scratching with the retrieved knowledge, SkinMind correctly identifies the condition as lichen amyloidosis. In contrast, Gemini-2.5-Flash and LightRAG select incorrect answers. This example illustrates how SkinMinds iterative evidence-seeking process supports fine-grained, evidence-grounded clinical reasoning.

sections.content: Figure 5 compares the average token consumption of SkinMind against five representative retrievalaugmented baselines on the Morph-R benchmark. The stacked bars show input and output tokens (left axis), while the line reports the average number of retrieved evidence tokens in the model context (right axis). Evidence efficiency. Most notably, SkinMind achieves the strongest task performance while using the fewest evidence tokens among all evaluated methods, averaging 1,380 tokens per question. By comparison, LightRAG uses 7,901 evidence tokens, 5.7 as many as SkinMind. This pattern suggests that SkinMinds gains are associated with more targeted evidence selection rather than larger retrieved context. Its hierarchical graph-probing interfaces support selective access to relevant textual and visual evidence at different levels of granularity. 11 SkinMind: Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Dermatology AI Reasoning-oriented token allocation. SkinMind allocates 21% of its token usage to model outputs, amounting to 5,576 tokens per question. These outputs include both the final answer and the intermediate decisions involved in navigating the graph and selecting evidence. In comparison, LightRAG allocates 2% of its token usage (291 tokens) to model outputs, with 11,802 input tokens consumed through upfront context construction. Aggregated across calls, total usage is approximately 26.1k tokens for SkinMind and 12.1k for LightRAG. SkinMinds multi-round inputs include the interaction history and tool instructions alongside retrieved evidence. This allocation characterizes its iterative evidence-acquisition process: the model progressively selects what to retrieve and uses the resulting observations to guide subsequent graph-probing actions. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced SkinMind, multimodal agentic RAG framework that interactively probes dermatology knowledge graph for textual, relational, and visual evidence. Equipped with hierarchical graph-probing tools, SkinMind interleaves reasoning with adaptive exploration of textual, relational, and visual evidence, progressively constructing query-specific evidence subgraphs. We also developed SkinMind-KG to provide comprehensive and traceable foundation of domain-specific knowledge. Across six dermatology VQA benchmarks and two policy models, SkinMind consistently outperforms direct answering and competing RAG methods while retrieving more targeted evidence. These results support adaptive graph probing as promising approach to evidence-grounded dermatology reasoning. sections.title: Appendix
sections.content: A SkinMind-KG Data Appendix This section documents the data-processing and graph-construction details that are abbreviated in the main paper. SkinMind-KG combines source-linked textual knowledge with image nodes under dermatology-specific schema. The construction pipeline preserves the source chunk identifiers associated with extracted entities and relations, thereby enabling retrieved graph content to be traced to its supporting text. A.1 Source Composition and Provenance The textual component of SkinMind-KG is constructed from 769 documents, including 227 clinical guidelines and 542 textbooks published since 2015. The multimodal component contains 423,016 images from Derm1M [39]. A.2 Text Parsing, Cleaning, and Chunking We parse each source document into page-level structured text using MinerU. Rule-based filtering removes non-textual elements, including images and tables, while incomplete adjacent paragraphs are merged. The processed text is then segmented into 1,200-token chunks with 100-token overlap for entity and relation extraction. Each chunk retains its document-level provenance and serves as the source unit associated with the extracted entities and relations. A.3 Disease Ontology and Extraction Schema We adopt the PanDerm ontology [40] as the taxonomic backbone of SkinMind-KG. It contains 127 dermatological disease concepts and their curated hierarchical relationships. We represent these concepts as Disease and DiseaseCategory nodes and encode their hierarchy using IS_SUBTYPE_OF relations. The resulting ontology is preloaded into SkinMind-KG before knowledge extraction. In consultation with senior dermatologists, we further define the 23 entity types in Table S1 and the 25 relation types in Table S2. Entities and relations are extracted from each text chunk using the system and user prompt templates reproduced in Section D. Relations are extracted using canonical sourcetarget roles, whereas the final graph is undirected and unweighted. A.4 Merging, Deduplication, and Conflict Resolution After extraction, records with the same entity name are grouped, duplicate source identifiers are removed, and relations connecting the same pair of nodes under the same relation type are consolidated. Self-loops are discarded. The grouping step is deterministic; an LLM is then used within each group to synthesize the collected descriptions and detect genuine factual conflicts. As specified by the prompt in Section D.5, two claims are considered conflicting only when their subject, attribute, clinical scope, metric, and unit match. Otherwise, their information is treated as complementary and integrated into single description. Integrating heterogeneous sources may introduce contradictory claims about the same entity or relation. When conflict is detected, the synthesis prompt preserves the opposing claims and generates targeted search queries without resolving the disagreement. Gemini-3.1-Pro subsequently uses these queries to retrieve relevant evidence through Google Search and determine whether the conflict can be resolved. This procedure processed 1,375 description-level conflicts, automatically resolving 1,366 (99.3%) and referring the remaining nine cases for expert review. 16 SkinMind: Appendix Table S1: Entity schema for constructing the textual subgraph of SkinMind-KG. sections.content: B.1 Hardware and Software Environment Experiments were run on eight NVIDIA A800-SXM4 GPUs with 80 GB of memory per GPU. sections.title: C Failure Case Analysis
sections.content: We also analyze two failure cases of SkinMind to examine its diagnostic reasoning and identify opportunities for more targeted evidence gathering. Both cases are drawn from the 25Cls benchmark [29], with Gemini-2.5-Flash [6] as the policy model. Figure S1 shows basal cell carcinoma (BCC) case predicted as keratoacanthoma (KA), while Figure S2 shows pilomatricoma predicted as cellular neurothekeoma. In both cases, SkinMind links retrieved disease knowledge to the lesions appearance. The first leaves growth history and central keratin unverified, while exploration in the second centers on the favored candidate. These observations suggest that the policy models agentic tool-use strategy could be further improved to gather evidence that better distinguishes competing diagnoses. Future work could explore tool-use training for agentic RAG to encourage more targeted tool selection and comparative exploration. Figure S1: Candidate differentiation after retrieval. Four of 25 options are shown. Numbered groups reorganize logged calls; red text marks retrospective analysis. SCC denotes squamous cell carcinoma. Figure S2: Candidate-focused exploration. sections.title: D Prompts and Tool Interfaces
sections.content: For reproducibility, this section reports the prompts and tool instructions used for knowledge-graph construction and SkinMind inference. During entity and relation extraction, {language} is set to English, {tuple_delimiter} to <#>, and {completion_delimiter} to <COMPLETE>. The {entity_ontology} and {relationship_ontology} placeholders are filled with the corresponding blocks shown below; {input_text} is replaced by the current source chunk. Precondition (mandatory): Two claims conflict ONLY if they describe the SAME fact under the SAME context. Before flagging, verify BOTH claims share the same: - Subject (same disease/drug/test/population) - Attribute (same dimension, e.g., both about first-line treatment, not first-line vs maintenance) - Scope (same severity, stage, site, treatment line, time frame) - Metric & unit (e.g., both 5-year survival, not survival vs response rate) If ANY differs, they are complementary -- set `has_conflict: false`. conflict IS: - Contradictory claims under fully matched context (e.g., "first-line for adult moderate plaque psoriasis is Drug A" vs "Drug B" for the same population) - Direct negation under matched context (e.g., "effective" vs "ineffective" for the same drug + indication) - Incompatible numerical values for the same metric, population, and unit conflict is NOT: - Different populations, severities, stages, sites, or treatment lines (e.g., "first-line for mild " vs "first-line for severe") - Different attributes (efficacy vs safety; diagnosis vs treatment) - Different granularity (general vs subtype-specific) - Different metrics, units, or time windows (1-year vs 5-year; absolute vs relative) - Wording differences with same meaning - One claim more specific or recent without explicit contradiction === TASK 2: Description Synthesis === Merge all descriptions into one comprehensive, objective summary.
